_sources: WHO Global Health Guidelines, ICMR Disease-specific Guidelines, MoHFW National Health Mission advisories. Generic lifestyle guidance only — no medication names, no dosages.
respiratory: Avoid exposure to tobacco smoke, indoor air pollution (e.g. burning biomass fuels), and dust — these are leading risk factors for respiratory infections per WHO guidelines.
Maintain good hand hygiene by washing hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, particularly before eating and after coughing or sneezing, to prevent transmission of respiratory pathogens.
Ensure adequate natural ventilation in living spaces; open windows regularly and avoid crowded enclosed areas during active outbreaks of respiratory illness.
Complete all recommended vaccinations including influenza and pneumococcal vaccines as advised by your doctor, especially if you are above 60 years, a child under 5, or have a chronic condition.
If diagnosed with or exposed to tuberculosis, complete the full course of treatment as prescribed and attend all follow-up visits — partial treatment leads to drug-resistant TB.
metabolic: Maintain a healthy body weight through regular moderate-intensity physical activity (at least 150 minutes per week) and a balanced diet low in refined sugars and saturated fats, as recommended by the Indian Council of Medical Research.
Reduce intake of processed foods, sweetened beverages, and white rice in favour of whole grains, pulses, green vegetables, and low-glycaemic-index foods to help regulate blood sugar levels.
Monitor fasting blood glucose regularly if you have a family history of diabetes, are overweight, or are above 40 years of age — early detection allows lifestyle management before progression.
Stay well hydrated with water or coconut water; avoid sugary drinks, as excess sugar intake is directly linked to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk.
Quit tobacco use in all forms — smoking and smokeless tobacco are independent risk factors for cardiovascular complications in people with diabetes.
cardiovascular: Limit daily sodium intake to less than 5 grams (approximately one teaspoon of salt) as recommended by WHO to reduce the risk of high blood pressure and its complications.
Engage in at least 30 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise (walking, cycling, swimming) on most days of the week to help maintain healthy blood pressure and heart function.
Manage stress through relaxation techniques such as yoga, deep breathing, or meditation — chronic psychological stress is associated with elevated blood pressure in Indian population studies.
Avoid tobacco in all forms and limit alcohol consumption; both are established risk factors for hypertension, stroke, and coronary artery disease.
Attend regular health check-ups including blood pressure measurement at least once a year if you are above 30 years, as hypertension is often asymptomatic until a serious event occurs.
general: Stay adequately hydrated (8–10 glasses of water per day) and maintain adequate rest — both support immune function and recovery from viral illnesses.
Practice food and water safety: consume only clean, treated drinking water and freshly cooked food, particularly during monsoon season when water-borne and vector-borne diseases are more common.
Use mosquito repellents, sleep under treated bed nets, and eliminate stagnant water around your home to prevent vector-borne diseases such as dengue and malaria.
Seek care early if symptoms worsen, last more than 3–5 days, or are accompanied by high fever, difficulty breathing, altered consciousness, or inability to retain fluids.
Maintain up-to-date immunisation records for yourself and your family as per the National Immunisation Schedule provided by MoHFW.
